          Make or Break for Renée Slegers? Man City Test Awaits Under-Pressure Arsenal Boss
        
      
                          
                      Oct 2, 2026
          
                      Maya Shah / Author, Emily Millen / Design, Yash Thakur / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Arsenal’s poor start has raised bigger questions than their results alone. We examine the data behind their lack of cutting edge ahead of a crucial trip to the Etihad on Sunday.

After finishing second in the Women's Super League last season, Arsenal would have been looking to build on their potential and bring home the title in 2027. However, with four matches played, the Gunners are already seven points behind leaders Manchester City in the league table.
Defeat to City this weekend would leave them 10 points off the top after only five matchdays. Arsenal have never trailed the league leaders by as much as 10 points after five games of a WSL season.
The same issues surfaced in Wednesday’s UEFA Women's Champions League 2-2 draw with Paris FC.

Arsenal had 69.5% possession and established a two-goal lead, but once again their control failed to translate into complete command of the game. Their performance in Paris highlighted a side still short on confidence and, at times, guilty of being their own worst enemy.

An inability to put the contest beyond doubt allowed Paris back into the match, with the French side generating 1.44 expected goals (xG) from open play compared to Arsenal's 1.16. While the penalty that sparked the comeback may have been unfortunate, the Gunners had already allowed Paris a foothold long before the equaliser arrived.

Given they've built their deepest squad in years with significant summer recruitment and have few injury concerns, not many would have thought Arsenal would have endured such a difficult start to the campaign.

They began with a hard-fought 1-0 win at Brighton, before a shock 0-0 home draw with newly-promoted Crystal Palace. Another game at the Emirates required a late equaliser against Manchester United, a late penalty against HB Køge saw them just about win their opening Champions League game, before suffering a 1-0 defeat at Chelsea last weekend.

The pre-season projection from the Opta supercomputer gave them a 25.6% chance of winning the WSL title across its 10,000 simulations; that figure has now fallen to 7.0%. A defeat at City on Sunday would leave their title hopes hanging by a thread.
Yet there is a familiar element to Arsenal’s struggles.

As was the case last season, the results are falling short of what the underlying numbers suggest. The Gunners' actual WSL points tally is already 2.4 points below their expected total this term, the second-largest underperformance in the league behind Brighton (5.9 points below).

Arsenal are averaging just 1.25 points per game, their lowest rate in any WSL season and are winless in three league matches. Only twice in their history have they endured a longer winless run in the competition, with four-game stretches in May 2014 and October 2023.

Their 97% field tilt against Crystal Palace was perhaps the clearest illustration. Arsenal dominated territory without translating that control into meaningful chances, recording the highest field tilt in a WSL match since the start of 2023-24.
For a team that went 20 WSL matches unbeaten before this run, the speed of the change is striking.

Arsenal are spending 54% of their playing time level — the highest proportion in the division, and a familiar sight for a team that accumulated eight draws last season out. Meanwhile, they have spent just 23% of games in a leading position, the eighth most in the WSL.

The question, then, is not simply whether Arsenal can recover their title challenge, but why a team with greater depth, significant recruitment and few injury concerns are once again struggling to turn control into results.
The most alarming aspect of Arsenal’s start is not simply that they are failing to score, but how little threat they are generating when they have the ball.
Sleger's side are dominating territory without consistently creating the openings that should follow.

The Gunners have scored just two goals from 78 shots across their four WSL matches. Only Charlton (1) have scored fewer goals, while Arsenal’s average of 39 shots per goal is currently the second-highest recorded by any team across a WSL season, behind only Yeovil Town in 2017-18 (46 per goal).
Indeed, Brighton are the only side underperforming their xG total by more than the Gunners – with a differential of -5.3 to the Gunners' -4.6.
